record_reviews.summary: Watson’s copied letter to Hooker argues that connecting intermediate plant forms are generally scarce, then tests that claim across varieties (Viola, Festuca), quasi-species (primrose/cowslip, Lysimachia), and species (Geum). He qualifies the rule with exceptional Circæa and Viola cases, describes three generations of Scotch Kail reverting toward a type, and gives a detailed cultivated Myosotis example whose forms shift between Azorica and maritima. This is third-party correspondence to Hooker, copied at Down and annotated by Darwin; it is not a Darwin-to-Watson or Watson-to-Darwin letter.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 12 April 1847 exact original date; copy made later, with date/salutation/signature in Darwin hand.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: H. C. Watson is author of the underlying prose; Hooker is recipient and Darwin’s copyist/annotator. Later Natural Selection references are editorial, not contemporaneous body voice.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin’s four-page draft thanks Watson for clarifying the large/small-genus problem with figures, discusses how artificial genus boundaries affect averages, and uses a submerged-hemisphere thought experiment to defend local flora as a fragmentary standard. record_reviews.summary: Watson replies to Darwin’s 26 August draft after a month of visitors. He argues Britain is a misleading local sample because small British genera can be large elsewhere, offers two competing diagrams for extreme-species distance, distinguishes numerical size from closeness, and explains how reproductive-character classification obscures total resemblance. Veronica, Mentha, Papaver, Fumaria and Rubus provide concrete contrasts.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 2 October 1855 exact day; the opening explicitly identifies Darwin’s 26 August letter, but does not give a postal receipt date.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Watson body only; diagrams and examples are his argument, while Darwin’s annotations and later Natural Selection citations are separate.
